articles.title: Iowa lead detonation: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite concerns - live updates
articles.summary: The army plans to detonate of 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500lbs of lead azide despite public concern about potential health and environmental effects

blocks.text: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals in Iowa despite concerns
The US military is set to deonate 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500lb of lead azide in Iowa at 10am Eastern time on Wednesday.
As the Guardian has previously reported, the army has changed the date three times after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa, where the plant is situated. The army has warned that the blast could release a plume of toxic lead dust extending up to 100 miles northeast, possibly reaching cities such as Wapello and New Boston, Illinois.
Last week, Iowa governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican, activated the state emergency management office, and the state created a website for information about the detonation.
Stick with us as we bring you the latest news from this planned detonation.
Key events

items: 2m agoIowa braces for blast that could spread lead plume over 100-mile radius
9m agoUS army map shows projected path of toxic dust from Iowa detonation
13m agoUS army to blow up bomb-making chemicals in Iowa despite concerns

blocks.text: Iowa braces for blast that could spread lead plume over 100-mile radius

The US Army is set to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

The controlled blast is planned to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes.
On Tuesday, the army released new maps forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri.

The army has warned that “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

The detonation is currently scheduled for 10am ET. In a public safety advisory released on Tuesday, the army said: “A more precise time will be communicated after evaluating changing weather patterns and waiting for the safest possible conditions.”
My colleague Cecilia Nowell has more here:
US army map shows projected path of toxic dust from Iowa detonation
Edward Helmore
The US army has released new maps showing the projected path of a toxic lead dust plume from the planned detonation of 68 barrels – five tons – of lead axide at an Iowa ammunition dump.
Projections show a plume moving south-west of the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, stretching through a south-eastern portion of the state before extending into northern Missouri.

The army sent an emergency notification to cellphones on Tuesday confirming the time of the controlled explosion – and warning that some people within five miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated.
The “imminent threat alert” told those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”.

The army said it had set up additional “blast barriers” around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated. It also said it would apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust and douse the explosive materials with thousands of gallons of water.

Acting secretary of the army Adam Telle said in a post on X that there was no reason for the public to panic. He said it was “unanimous judgment” of various government entities that the army “should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation”.

articles.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
articles.summary:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists…

blocks.text: A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

blocks.caption: An African forest elephant. Photograph: Danita Delimont/Alamy

blocks.text: Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.
after newsletter promotion

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

articles.title: US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 others
articles.summary: The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high…

image.caption: US President Donald Trump speaks at a press conference in February after the Supreme Court struck down his global tariffs [FILE: February 20, 2026]Image: Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled new tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
A senior US official said the proposed duties follow a months-long investigation into allegations that excessive manufacturing abroad puts American producers at a disadvantage.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, although some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

China would face an additional tariff of 20%, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%. The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, according to a senior US administration official.
Other affected economies include India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam.
The tariffs could take effect in January at the earliest, following a public comment period.
Why is Trump planning new tariffs?
The measures are also intended to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down US president Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.

The proposed duties could further fuel US inflation, which reached 3.7% in September. High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.
The tariff plans come just weeks before Trump is due to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
The US official played down concerns about renewed trade tensions and said Washington could sign further trade agreements at the summit.

articles.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
articles.summary:
Honours students are increasingly being asked to sit oral assessments – but at the University of Sydney it’s become a requirement for all

  • Get our

blocks.text: When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.
Top Australian universities are increasingly asking honours students to sit oral assessments, with Sydney the first known to require it across honours programs.

Exams have moved from computers back to paper or interviews in the four years since the release of ChatGPT made AI plagiarism a concern. Some educators have adopted the debate-focused tutorials traditional at Oxbridge colleges or the viva voce assessments typical of PhDs.

But honours programs – a year of intensive research for dedicated students after their bachelor’s degree – have been slower to adapt as they’re typically focused on a single project, which accounts for most of their grade.

Elwig Pollock, a history student, said he had not used AI at all on his work on how the commemoration of Captain Cook has evolved over time, and that the new demand was “insulting” to students and the professors who supervise them.

“If you’ve used AI to do your honours thesis and your supervisor has not figured it out throughout your regular meetings, then what’s stopping you from communicating that material successfully in a 15-minute conversation,” Elwig Pollock said.

blocks.caption: Elwig Pollock sat for a short pass or fail conversation, but it is worth 0% of his grade as most marks come from his thesis. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Since 2024, Sydney bachelor’s degrees have included a mix of assessments that are vulnerable or secure to AI tools. This year, the university has formally extended that to honours programs, though the format is different for every faculty.

On Wednesday, Elwig Pollock had a short conversation which was a pass or fail hurdle task but was worth nothing towards his final grade. In his case most of his marks are coming from his thesis but his degree will not be awarded if he fails the conversation.
Engineering student Isabelle* had an entirely different experience.

Last week, the University of Sydney student had an hour of interviews with professors in a single room with five classmates, as the school rushed through assessing 250 students in two days. It accounted for 50% of her grade.
Her 20,000-word thesis was worth just 20%.
“There were people coming in and out of the room while we were being assessed so it was distracting,” said Isabelle, who asked for a pseudonym to avoid being penalised.
“[We had to] move to the other side of the room so my marker could hear me.”

The change has stressed students who aren’t used to speaking up in class, don’t speak English as a first language or need their honours to become qualified in their field – including engineers like Isabelle.
“I think it’s particularly bad in engineering because writing skills are poor, but I think it’s a Band-Aid solution,” she said of the verbal component.
Adam Bridgeman, the university’s acting deputy vice-chancellor for education, said honours degrees needed to change.
“We necessarily treat honours theses as open assessments as we can’t reliably restrict AI use,” Bridgeman said.
after newsletter promotion
Staff and students were offered guidance and practice to manage the transformation and ensure English fluency and speaking ability were not “inadvertently rewarded”, he said.
“We appreciate some students might be nervous about the experience, especially if it’s their first time,” Bridgeman said. “We’ll take feedback on board as we plan for 2027 assessments.”

While Sydney is the only major institution to mandate interviews for honours programs, schools at the University of Melbourne, Monash University and Australian Catholic University are bringing them in.

Adelaide University, which was previously among the first in Australia to reintroduce viva voce tasks, is using “interactive oral assessments” in which students and teachers role-play real-world professional situations.

There are no public reports of Australian honours students cheating with AI. Kurt Iveson, an honours coordinator for Sydney’s School of Geosciences, said the change was still needed to respond to AI’s growing role in education.
“They’re not the kind of people that I would personally be worried about getting Claude to write their honours thesis for them,” Iveson said.
“But … [management] want to be able to demonstrate to the world, as part of their social licence and external accreditation, that things are being assessed securely.”

The interviews are a heavy addition to professors’ workloads – and no casuals have been brought on to help. Staff and students contacted by Guardian Australia said the new rules had left supervisors feeling rushed and overworked.
But, Iveson said, interviews are a valuable way of helping students learn and understand the significance of their research.
“Assuming that you have actually written it, you know your shit, you’ll be fine, and you’ll have a good conversation.”

articles.title: Labour ‘committed’ to ban on conversion practices despite calls for proposed law to be scrapped
articles.summary: Exclusive: Campaigners say new legislation in England and Wales could infringe on free speech, parenting and religious freedom

blocks.text: Labour is “committed” to banning conversion practices despite growing calls to amend or scrap the proposed law over fears it could stifle free speech, the equalities minister has said.

Bridget Phillipson said there was “no question as to the principle of the bill” and that “normal parenting will not be affected” by the law, which would ban abuse that aims to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity in England and Wales.

“The principle of this is the right one,” she said. “There’s a reason we put it in our manifesto. We made a choice to publish a draft bill for further discussion and we welcome all feedback but there’s no question as to the principle of the bill, which is that we shouldn’t be treating LGBT people in an abusive way in modern society.”

The draft bill, published in June, proposes that people found guilty of conversion practices face an unlimited fine and up to five years in prison. Courts would also be able to issue conversion practice protection orders before serious harm occurs if an individual is deemed at risk of being subjected to an abusive practice, including being taken abroad.

However, the bill has prompted criticism from religious leaders and the former head of Britain’s rights watchdog, with calls for the legislation to be abandoned. Opponents argue harmful practices are already covered in law, and that the bill could threaten parental and religious rights.
The government and proponents of the bill were dealt a blow last week when Hilary Cass, the paediatrician behind a review into children’s gender services, withdrew her support.

Cass, who sits in the House of Lords and was initially quoted in a government press release announcing the bill, said she could no longer support it without radical changes, which she suggested might not be possible.

“The draft bill is already having a chilling effect on healthcare professionals who fear they may be accused of falling far below professional standards, even when they have conducted appropriate and ethical therapy,” she said, giving evidence to a joint committee of MPs and peers scrutinising the bill.

Phillipson said she was grateful for Cass’s feedback and was taking it seriously, adding: “I know the committee will be reflecting on her evidence to make sure that when we bring forward final legislation, we do it in the right way so that parents and healthcare professionals are able to have open and frank conversations on this topic.”

Kai O’Doherty, from anti-LGBT abuse charity Galop, said opponents of the bill had been “creating scenarios we don’t recognise as being conversion practices, and detracting from the actual victims and survivors who are trying to seek protection so others don’t have to suffer what they had to experience”.

They added: “The harm threshold is very high so the opposition to the bill is disingenuous in presenting it as causing any risk of inadvertently criminalising parents or people in the workplace. There are some ways in which the bill is already weaker than international comparators, so it’s critical it does not get watered down.”

Simon Blake, CEO of Stonewall, said some of the examples being given by opponents were “clearly scaremongering”. “Open noise conversations and disagreements between parents and children won’t be captured,” he said. “We know that health professionals and counsellors have a job that needs to be done, and need to ask robust questions. What they don’t have is a right to try to change somebody based on a predetermined view about their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

The legislation follows years of failed attempts by successive Conservative governments to introduce a ban. Theresa May first pledged to outlaw conversion practices in 2018, as did Boris Johnson in 2019.

Johnson briefly abandoned the plans in 2022 before reversing course after a backlash, but he proposed excluding transgender people from the ban. Rishi Sunak later promised to bring forward legislation, but this did not happen before the Conservatives left office in 2024.

Helen Joyce, director of advocacy at gender-critical campaign group Sex Matters, said: “We want the bill to be withdrawn, not because we want people to be able to commit abuse with impunity, but because the proponents have not demonstrated a need for it, and it will cause an immense amount of collateral damage.”
Joyce argued that what most people think of as a “conversion practice”, such as violence, confinement, sexual assault and physical and psychological abuse, is already a criminal offence.

She said the previous government had made genuine efforts to introduce a ban but struggled to draft legislation that would protect people from abuse without infringing on established human rights, such as freedom of belief and expression, parental authority and protections for family life.

The Church of England has supported a ban on conversion practices relating to sexual orientation since 2017, but a spokesperson said legislation must not “unintentionally criminalise providing appropriate prayer and pastoral care to those who seek it”.
The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales has called for the bill to be abandoned.

Nathan Stilwell, from Humanists UK, said: “Cass is right that it is important we get these definitions right, and they aren’t used vexatiously and wrongly. But what is missing from Cass’s intervention is the experience of people who’ve gone through these conversion practices.”

articles.title: Annual US consumer price inflation hits 3.8% – highest level since May
articles.summary:
Rise occurs amid soaring energy prices, according to last inflation reading before a crucial Fed board meeting

Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, according to new inflation…

blocks.text: Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, according to new inflation data released on Wednesday, the highest since May and the last inflation reading before a crucial US Federal Reserve board meeting next month.

Prices rose 0.3% from September to October amid soaring energy prices, according to the Personal Consumption Expenditure index, the Fed’s preferred inflation measure from the commerce department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis.
The data comes after the Bureau of Labor Statistics separately reported prices climbed 0.4% from September to October, higher than economists had anticipated.
Energy prices, including gas prices at the pump, have cooled, going from a high of $4.41 a gallon in early October to $3.61 a gallon by mid-November, according to AAA.

In early December, the Fed will hold the last of its interest rate-setting meetings for the year, and officials are widely expected to hike interest rates for the second time this year. The Fed has set a target inflation rate of 2%, a level not seen since February 2021. Higher interest rates make it more expensive to borrow money, slowing price increases and raising the price of loans like mortgages and student debt.
Though officials held rates steady at the last board meeting in late October, minutes from the meeting showed that some expressed concern about inflation’s stickiness.
“A few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later,” the minutes said.

The move would come at a tumultuous time for the US economy. A new survey from the Conference Board released on Tuesday showed consumer confidence had ticked up in November to its highest level since January 2025, probably driven by the shake-up from the midterm elections.

At the same time, US stocks have been fluctuating from a mixture of uncertainty over datacenter regulations, continuing scandals coming out of Nvidia and overall investor concern about the seemingly limitless amount of money being spent on building AI and the infrastructure to support it.

articles.title: EU plans €50 billion sovereign tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
articles.summary: The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.

image.caption: Quantum computing technology is still in the early stages of developmentImage: Ross D. Franklin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.

"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound ​impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
Will quantum computers destroy the internet?
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
Are quantum computers creating a new future?
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.

Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies

Around one-third of the world's quantum companies ⁠are ​based in the European Union, according to ​the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

articles.title: Number of women killed by men in Ireland almost doubles in a year
articles.summary:
Figures from past 30 years show more than half of victims killed by current or ex-partner

The number of women in Ireland killed by men…

blocks.text: The number of women in Ireland killed by men has surged in the past five years and risen especially sharply in the past 12 months, according to a study.
After falling for two decades, the number of violent deaths began going up in 2021 and has risen sharply this year, with 13 deaths so far, the report by Irish charity Women’s Aid said on Wednesday.
“That should alarm every one of us,” said Sarah Benson, the organisation’s chief executive. “After years of decline, the number of women killed is rising again.”

The vast majority of victims over the past three decades were killed by a man they knew and over half were killed by a current or former partner. The findings match UN and EU data showing the most dangerous place for a woman is her own home, and the most likely killer is a man she knows, said Benson.

“Ireland is one of the wealthiest countries in the world, and we have good laws. Yet women are still being killed by the men closest to them. Most men choose never to behave this way, and that is exactly why we need everyone to recognise this violence and call it out.”
Since 1996, when the Dublin-based charity began collating femicide statistics, 291 women have been killed by men.

Measured in five-year blocks, the levels of violent deaths peaked at 67 between 1996 and 2000 and fell to a low of 31 between 2016 and 2020. During the 2021–2025 period, 40 deaths were recorded, a 29% increase on the previous period.
The 13 women who died in violent circumstances this year is almost double the figure of seven for all of last year.
However, Ireland’s overall murder rate of 0.66 per 100,000 people remains well below global and European averages. The country has a population of 5.5 million.

Of the 235 cases of violent deaths resolved since 1996, 89% of the women were killed by a man known to them, 57% were killed by a current or former partner, 32% by a male relative or acquaintance and 11% by a male stranger. More than two-thirds – 68% – died in their own homes. Just over a quarter were women aged 26 to 35.

“Intimate partner femicide rarely comes out of nowhere,” said Benson. “Separation, coercive control, non-fatal strangulation, threats to kill and stalking are all known warning signs. When a woman tells Women’s Aid that she is afraid for her life, we believe her.”

Leaving an abusive partner did not always end abuse, said Benson. “Risk rises sharply around separation and stays high for about a year. For every woman whose life is taken, thousands more are living on a knife’s edge of fear.”
The Femicide Watch report, which coincided with International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, recorded that 25 children were killed alongside a woman, usually their mother.

articles.title: Ice hockey prospect Max Calce follows Leon Draisaitl's path, leaving Mannheim for Canada
articles.summary: The player widely seen as Germany's biggest ice hockey talent to come along in years is leaving the country's top professional league for Canada – changing tracks in his bid to make it to the NHL.

image.caption: As he is still under 18, Max Calce had to wear a full cage during DEL gamesImage: Udo Herrmann/Herrmann Agenturfotografie/IMAGO

blocks.text: Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.
"I have long had three goals," he said. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home."
Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.
The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.

This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.
Mature decision-making on the ice
"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," said former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.
"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision."
Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.

blocks.caption: Max Calce was named player of the game after scoring his first goal for GermanyImage: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.
"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person."
This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.
"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director said.
"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition."
Increased visibility ahead of NHL draft

On the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.

In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.

This, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.
Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

articles.title: BBC lodges urgent appeal against Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit
articles.summary:
Corporation asks US court of appeals for the 11th circuit to throw out case brought over Panorama documentary

The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation…

blocks.text: The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against it thrown out, after internal surprise at a judge’s decision to allow the case to go to trial.
The corporation is currently heading to court next year over a Panorama documentary that spliced together two parts of Trump’s speech made before the 6 January insurrection at the US Capitol.

While the broadcaster has apologised over the edit, which featured in the 2024 programme Trump: A Second Chance, it has always denied that the film defamed Trump. It has also said it was never broadcast in Florida, where Trump’s legal action is being heard.

The federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump appointee, ruled earlier this month that the lawsuit could proceed, denying the BBC’s attempt to have the case thrown out. However, the BBC has now appealed to a higher court, the United States court of appeals for the 11th circuit, restating that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.

In a legal submission seen by the Guardian, the BBC’s lawyers state that the documentary “never aired in the United States”. It argues that Kuntz found the Florida court held jurisdiction over the BBC “despite the complete lack of evidence that anyone accessed it there, as both Florida law and this circuit’s precedent require”.

The move is a sign of the BBC’s desperation to have the case dismissed, given the time, expense and political headache it is causing, while it is also making huge cuts at home and holding talks with the UK government over its future funding.

“We are surprised and disappointed by the court’s decision that this case should be heard in Florida,” said a BBC spokesperson. “As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK – and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.
“Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling.”
The spliced clip suggested that Trump told a crowd: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you, and we fight. We fight like hell.”
The words were taken from sections of his speech almost an hour apart.

Kuntz was nominated to his current role by Trump and confirmed by a Senate vote earlier this year, which split down party lines, Republicans in favour, with Democrat and independent senators voting against the appointment. Three senators did not vote.

Kuntz ruled earlier this month that Trump had sufficiently pleaded “actual malice” on behalf of the BBC’s editing. “Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” he wrote.
after newsletter promotion
On his Truth Social site, Trump described the ruling as a “huge victory against fake news BBC”.

In its appeal, the BBC’s legal team states that the Florida court “ignored the BBC’s rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary and its other streaming content in the United States”.

“This erroneous exercise of jurisdiction over the BBC is anathema to the due process requirements of personal jurisdiction and to the comity interests in allowing other sovereign nations to police their own affairs,” it states.

“The BBC did not produce, film, or air the documentary in Florida. Rather, the BBC aired it on its UK TV channels, and also made it available on the UK iPlayer streaming service. The BBC never broadcast it in the US, nor did it have the rights to do so. Third parties acquired the international distribution rights … though they never aired it in the US.”
Trump himself is still due to give a deposition in the case, a process in which he is questioned by lawyers under oath. However, it has been postponed until January.

articles.title: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK next year
articles.summary: US retail giant links up with Hyundai in attempt to crack £200bn British market

blocks.text: Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market.
The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from Korean manufacturer Hyundai. It will be the first time the US tech company has sold cars outside its home country.

Amazon, which is the world’s biggest online retailer with a market value of $2.7tn (£2.1tn), started selling cars at the end of 2024 in an effort to expand into one of the few remaining major consumer markets it had not already targeted.
Its latest move will be watched closely by car retailers that share a UK market worth more than £200bn a year.
Amazon Autos operates in 150 US cities and counts thousands of dealers in its networks, offering vehicles from 35 brands.

UK buyers will be able to buy new electric hybrid and petrol Hyundai models, as well as used cars from Vertu Motors, a large British dealership. Amazon said customers would be able to explore financing options before reserving a car and completing the purchase in physical dealerships. More brands and dealers will be announced before the launch of the UK service.
Amazon will go up against online new and used dealers, as well as traditional physical dealerships. Car companies also sell directly to consumers through their websites.
The share price of Autotrader, the UK’s largest car sales website and a member of the FTSE 100, fell 2% on Wednesday after news of Amazon’s move.
Vertu’s share price rose 4% although it also announced acquisitions of dealerships. The company, listed on London’s Alternative Investment Market, was valued at £269m before the announcement.

Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International, said: “Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon.
after newsletter promotion
“In the UK, that means making it easy for customers to browse available cars, see upfront pricing, reserve the car and connect with the dealer to finalise the purchase.”

Hyundai was also the first brand to work with Amazon in the US. José Muñoz, its chief executive, said: “Our partnership with Amazon Autos has changed the way many customers discover Hyundai in the US, and 78% of the Amazon-influenced sales at our dealerships have come from customers who are new to our brand.”
Robert Forrester, Vertu’s chief executive, said his company was “committed to meeting customers wherever they choose to begin their buying journey”.

articles.title: Why Indians are still ending up in Russia's war
articles.summary: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?

image.caption: Modi raised Russian recruitment of Indians when they met in Moscow in July 2024 [FILE]Image: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.
But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.
After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.

In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.
Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India.

He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.
Ukraine war: Plight of Indians trapped in Russian army
India's efforts to bring recruits home
The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.
At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.

In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.
The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.

The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.
Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.
Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine
Duped or desperate?
Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.
"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.
He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.

"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.

The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.
Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.
He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.
"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.
Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.

Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.
"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.
He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.
India's special relationship with Russia explained
Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy
India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.

The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.
Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.
He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.
"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.
Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.
"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

articles.title: Plane crash off coast of Mississippi kills six, including two children
articles.summary:
Divers recover bodies after Cessna 210 went down in Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday afternoon killing all onboard

Divers have found the bodies of six people killed in

blocks.text: Divers have found the bodies of six people killed in a small plane crash on Tuesday off the coast of Mississippi, according to the US Coast Guard.

Their bodies were in the plane’s fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands national seashore. Four adults and two boys, ages eight and 10, were onboard, a Coast Guard spokesperson, Juan Ros, said.

The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported about 3.45pm that it lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. Responders searched for hours and initially only found three lifejackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard coordinator for search and rescue in the Mobile area, called the situation heartbreaking.

“While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families,” he said in a statement.
The New Orleans news station WVUE reported that those onboard the crashed plane were traveling back home after a fishing trip in Venice, Louisiana.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will investigate the crash.
On 3 November, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

articles.title: Justice Leonen concurs with dismissal but says SC should have ruled on Duterte arrest
articles.summary: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the…

blocks.text: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the International Criminal Court but stressed that the court should have also ruled its legality

In his 58-page concurring and dissenting opinion, Leonen agreed to dismiss the petitions for mootness, yet dissented from the majority's failure to “address unresolved, grave, and serious constitutional questions that can recur yet may evade judicial review.”

“I concur in the finding that the Petition for Habeas Corpus should be dismissed. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has competence to determine its own jurisdiction, which includes the disposition of any person physically surrendered to it,” Leonen said.

“However, I dissent from the Court's failure to provide clear guidance for future cases. The situation involves clear, serious, and grave constitutional issues that are capable of repetition and would otherwise evade review. Our silence can be interpreted as complicity in a violation of the Constitution, our concurrence with a treaty, and the relevant law,” he added.
Leonen said that by leaving these questions unanswered, the high court failed to provide much-needed guidelines for future cases.

“The constitutional issues raised in the present Petitions are grave and serious and capable of repetition, yet evading review. This case cannot simply be dismissed on the ground of mootness, even if doing so may be the politically expedient resolution,” Leonen said.

“As the Court of last resort, we must not shirk our duty of providing the clearest guidelines, for the bench and the bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies. That is the resolution that would best safeguard and operationalize the human rights provisions under the Rome Statute, which are read through our Constitution,” he added.

Pointing to the risk of similar incidents happening again, Leonen said that Duterte’s purported co-perpetrators remain at large in Philippine territory and “may, at any time, be seized by Philippine authorities and surrendered in the same manner” as the former president.
“In the present case, the manner in which petitioner was seized and surrendered, if repeated in a future case, would evade judicial review,” Leonen said.
The former President was arrested on March 25, 2025 and taken to the Scheveningen prison in The Hague on a warrant of arrest from the ICC.

Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder in connection with the deaths under his war on drugs when he was president of the Philippines and mayor of Davao City.

In separate petitions filed in March 2025, Duterte's youngest daughter Kitty and her half-brothers Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte and Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte asked the SC to order the government to present the former President before the High Court.
The Duterte camp said that the ICC arrest warrant cannot be used as the basis for the arrest and detention of the former president, claiming that it has no jurisdiction in the Philippines.
It said that the ICC may only exercise its jurisdiction if the country’s legal system is not functioning, stressing that the Philippine judicial system is working.
The Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, in 2019 after the Hague-based tribunal began a probe into the Duterte administration's drug war.
Kitty will appeal the decision of the SC.
Duterte's trial before the ICC will start on Nov. 30, 2026.
'Violated rights, equal protection'
Leonen criticized the failure to subject the ICC arrest warrant to Philippine judicial review.

He noted that Duterte should have been promptly brought before a national court—where his identity, the regularity of the arrest, and the observance of his constitutional rights could be confirmed—before any surrender abroad.
Leonen added that the same court should have ensured the arrested person understood their rights and had a genuine opportunity to exercise them, especially when applying for interim release.

“The principal constitutional defect lay not in the absence of a fresh determination of probable cause–that question belonged to the issuing international court or tribunal—but in the total absence of any judicial review: former President Duterte was taken and flown to The Hague within hours, without any judicial imprimatur sought by his captors," Leonen said.
"That omission was a real violation of his right to be free from seizure except through judicial process,” he added.

Leonen acknowledged that surrendering Duterte and his former lieutenants has its advantages, but stressed that doing so does not represent complete accountability and should not stop the court from scrutinizing the process.

“Insisting on respect for human rights is not advancing a political cause or placing anyone beyond the reach of prosecution. It is insisting that justice be pursued through means worthy of its name-humane in application and legitimate in exercise,” Leonen said.

“A proper legal and just procedure for everyone matters. The procedure that protects a former president is the same procedure that protects the farmer taken at night and the young father picked up in an operation in a crowded barangay. Whatever we refuse to the powerful, we will soon be unable to guarantee to the powerless,” he added.
Dissenting opinions

The justices who voted against dismissing the petitions were Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando, retired Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, Associate Justice Henri Jean Paul Inting and Associate Justice Antonio Kho Jr., according to the SC.

Hernando argued that Duterte’s surrender to the ICC violated constitutional rights including due process, protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, freedom of travel, and the rights of persons under custodial investigation.
He added that the former president’s surrender through Republic Act No. 9851 is unconstitutional.

Meanwhile, Lazaro-Javier rejected the majority’s view that the petitions had become moot, pointing out that the cases question the conduct of Philippine authorities rather than the ICC’s current custody of Duterte.
She explained that the legality of the respondent law enforcement officers’ acts—the arrest, detention, and rendition of Duterte to the ICC—is separate from the ICC’s custody.

She further stressed that a writ of habeas corpus examines not just physical detention, but also its legality and the constitutional principles involved, adding that the Executive branch’s decision not to seek Duterte’s repatriation remains open to judicial review.

For his part, Inting noted that determining whether the arrest and surrender followed the Philippine Constitution and domestic laws is a legal issue for the courts to resolve, not a political question left solely to the executive or legislative branches.

“The case continues to present a controversy on whether FPRRD was validly arrested and detained by the Philippine authorities on March 11, 2025, when he was surrendered to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC). The issue is not a purely political question and should be resolved by the Court,” Inting said.

He also mentioned that an SC ruling could have practical value for ICC proceedings and case law, particularly under the abuse of process doctrine, where the ICC may suspend or terminate proceedings if improper or unlawful procedures were used to carry out an otherwise lawful process, such as an ICC arrest warrant.
'Sans domestic law, court authority'

Finally, Kho argued that the government cannot surrender a Filipino citizen to a foreign tribunal, or carry out an “extraordinary rendition,” without a valid domestic law and prior authority from the courts.
“Absent any such domestic law and prior judicial authorization, the extraordinary rendition of FPRRD to the ICC by the Philippine government is unconstitutional per se,” Kho said.

He also pointed out that if the SC were to dismiss the petitions as moot simply because Duterte had already been surrendered, similar actions in the future could evade judicial review just by being carried out quickly.

In March 2025, Duterte was transferred to the custody of the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands. He is set to stand trial for crimes against humanity before the ICC starting November 30, 2026. —NB, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: ‘This is political oppression’: Native Americans accuse Massachusetts town in Thanksgiving dispute
articles.summary:
Plymouth, where Pilgrims settled, accused of breaking 28-year old agreement over National Day of Mourning protest

Nearly 30 years after a violent clash between Native Americans and police,…

blocks.text: Nearly 30 years after a violent clash between Native Americans and police, the Massachusetts town of Plymouth is in court accused of “silencing” their National Day of Mourning – again.
A Native American group won a “mixed” victory over the historic Massachusetts town of Plymouth after they sued them for breaking a 30-year-old ‘treaty’ involving their National Day of Mourning.

On Monday, the United American Indians of New England (UAINE) attended Plymouth superior court in the latest stage of a year-long dispute over who would fund the annual memorial, and whether Native Americans must “ask permission to protest on stolen land”.

While the judge ruled partially in their favour on Tuesday, Mahtowin Munro, an Oglala Lakota and co-leader of UAINE, warned that the fight was settler colonialism hiding behind “red tape” and that they did not expect justice from “the courts of colonizers”.

Jean-Luc Pierite, president of the North American Indian Centre of Boston (Naicob), told the Guardian: “This is political oppression. This is about holding government agencies to account for breach of contract, for breaking treaties.”

The National Day of Mourning (NDOM) was founded in 1970 by Wamsutta Frank James, a member of the federally recognised Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) on Martha’s Vineyard, after he was uninvited from speaking at the state’s 350th anniversary of the Mayflower landing over his critical views.

For 50 years, as millions of Americans sit down to a turkey dinner, hundreds of Indigenous people and allies have gathered peacefully at noon on Cole’s Hill above Plymouth Rock in what is known as “America’s Hometown”, founded by the Pilgrims in 1620 on the ancestral Wampanoag homeland of Patuxet.

At the NDOM, food is shared, stories are told, and banners are paraded through the streets commemorating millions of Native Americans killed by European settlers, the theft of land, and the erasure of culture, as well as challenging Thanksgiving “myths”. UAINE call it a “solemn, spiritual and highly political day”.

In 1997, violence broke out. Town and state police were accused of pepper-spraying marchers, injuring elders, and arresting 25 people. Video footage from that day shows police hand-cuffing and dragging people.

A civil lawsuit ended in a 1998 out-of-court settlement allegedly amounting to $135,000 in which Plymouth agreed not to impede future NDOM protests, to provide a mobile stage, and to not require the organisation to ask for “permission to protest on stolen land”, including permits and prior notice.

In a statement at the time, UAINE said: “Plymouth has acknowledged our right to walk on our own land without a permit on National Day of Mourning. Plymouth has agreed to make the truth part of its celebration of the pilgrim myth of Thanksgiving … We are confident that this agreement represents a tremendous victory for the struggle of Native people to have our voices heard and respected.”
That all changed in 2025, when the town’s select board voted to renege on the agreement, and was overruled in court.

Munro said they suspected the town were “throwing up roadblocks because they don’t want the tourists to see or hear Native Americans who are speaking about the true history of the Pilgrim invasion and resulting land theft and genocide of Wampanoag and other Native peoples”.

On 10 November, 16 days before Thanksgiving, the board voted unanimously in a private meeting to breach the long-standing agreement again and demand the group obtain insurance to indemnify the town at a cost of several hundred dollars.

UAINE’s lawyers filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, and on Monday, local supporters of UAINE gathered outside holding signs that read “Selectmen – stop abusing Plymouth’s first citizens” and “Stop breaking treaties”.
Judge Brian Glenny heard 90 minutes of arguments. He is expected to issue a ruling soon.

During the hearing, the original agreement wording was dissected minutely. Plymouth’s lawyers argued that it does not specifically mention insurance and that UAINE should apply for it, like other organisers of public events. They added that the “showmobile” – the mobile stage cited in the original agreement – is dilapidated, and the town declined to continue providing a replacement from its own staging equipment, as it had done since 2014.

In a statement, Plymouth said that the town “supports and respects the constitutional rights to freedom of speech and peaceful assembly”. It said it had attempted to find a solution for a year but did not receive a reply from UAINE lawyers until August.

It added: “The town has gone above and beyond to accommodate UAINE’s event, including facilitating accessible parking, assisting elders, identifying locations for meals and extended observances, and coordinating with police and fire officials. The town has continuously demonstrated a willingness to address concerns, offer solutions, and make accommodations at every opportunity. These efforts reflect a genuine commitment to the event.”
after newsletter promotion

In turn, UAINE accused Plymouth of ripping up a 28-year-old political contract, violating its freedom of speech and attempting to force the group, which had been guaranteed the right to choose its own route, to gather at a new location, where members would be “out of sight”.
Plymouth denies trying to change the route and said the offer of the move was based on accessibility, parking, and the use of an existing stage in that location.

After hearing arguments on Monday, Judge Brian Glenny of Plymouth superior court ruled on Tuesday that the 1998 agreement was legally binding and banned the town from requiring insurance or permits for the event.

But he also absolved Plymouth from providing a stage, as it had done for 27 years. The ruling also appeared to open a path for Plymouth to challenge the 1998 agreement again in the future by stating that the 10 Novembervote was legal.
Munro called the ruling “mixed” and vowed to go ahead with this year’s protest.

She said: “Settlers frequently break their agreements with Indigenous peoples. In fact, the US has broken every single treaty it signed with Native Nations. And we know that we can’t count on the courts of the colonizers to give us justice.”
In a statement, Deb Iaquinto, Plymouth select board chair, said: “The Town has tried to work collaboratively to support UAINE’s rights to freedom of speech and assembly.”
She added: “In light of this ruling, the Town remains committed to supporting the National Day of Mourning.”

Pierite, whose organisation Naicob is the commonwealth’s designated liaison for members of the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Mi’kmaq, and Maliseet tribes, said the insistence on bureaucracy was being weaponised to erase their unique relationship and history with the town and the United States, and that Native Americans were not just “any other group” holding a parade.

Pierite, a member of the federally recognised Tunica-Biloxi tribe of Louisiana, added: “This isn’t about resiliency of Indigenous peoples. We are going to find a way for National Day of Mourning to happen, but we do need to make sure they are held accountable for this 1998 agreement. Plymouth itself has been a site of government relationships since April 1621 with the original treaty with [Chief] Massasoit [a defensive alliance between Europeans and Wampanoag lasting 50 years].
“Treaties have been endlessly interpreted and reinterpreted over centuries. This is one part of a very long fight.”

articles.title: King tides coincide with storms across coastal B.C. as evacuation alerts issued
articles.summary: Many coastal communities of B.C. are preparing with sandbags and clearing debris as a king tide coincides with waves of heavy rain and wind on Wednesday.

image.caption: High tides are seen in Delta's Boundary Bay on Tuesday. King tides are coinciding with storms hitting coastal B.C. through the middle of the week, with communities like Delta preparing with sandbags. (Hunter Soo/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
Many coastal communities of B.C. are preparing with sandbags and clearing debris as a king tide coincides with waves of heavy rain and wind on Wednesday.
Coastal flooding warnings cover swath of coastal B.C. as communities prepare with sandbags
Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) issued coastal flooding warnings for the west coast of Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, along with parts of the Central Coast.
The forecaster said that storm surges would lead to water levels 0.2 to 0.5 metres higher than usual on Wednesday and Thursday.

Some Vancouver Island communities, including the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and Parksville, issued evacuation alerts for low-lying areas as they prepared for the high tides to hit over the upcoming days.
In Metro Vancouver, the City of Delta said earlier this week it was "taking proactive steps to prepare low-lying coastal neighbourhoods for flood mitigation and response."
Meanwhile, in the Sea-to-Sky region, a state of local emergency was put in place in Squamish, which was significantly affected by storms earlier this month.
Low-pressure system drenches Vancouver Island
Squamish Mayor Sean Easton said the high tides were going to combine with high water levels from those storms.
"As part of the state of emergency, we are taking proactive measures and doing sandbagging ... and doing impromptu or proactive diking," he said late Tuesday.
Easton said the district was paying close attention to certain areas that were affected by king tides in 2022, and was particularly helping unhoused residents living in an encampment along waterways.
"It's an example of these extreme weather events really impacting directly, in this case, marginalized communities," he said.
The district said people should stay clear of rivers and not drive across flooded roads, as the B.C. River Forecast Centre issued high streamflow advisories for Vancouver Island and the South Coast.
An ECCC meteorologist told CBC News that one storm system passed through coastal B.C. on Tuesday, and another one is expected to hit late Wednesday.
Highway 16 on Haida Gwaii was closed on Tuesday due to debris and water on the road, according to DriveBC. (DriveBC)

The Transportation Ministry said in a Tuesday traffic advisory that communities along Highway 101 on the Sunshine Coast and Howe Sound, as well as those along the Malahat Highway on the west coast of Vancouver Island, were likely to be most affected by the incoming weather.
Other communities on Vancouver Island, like Tofino and Ucluelet, said public beach access would be closed due to the incoming storms.

items: How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.

blocks.text: A king tide refers to a phenomenon where cosmic alignments can mean dramatic tides, which can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average high tide mark.

The current king tide is expected to end on Thursday, but up until then, officials are warning people along the coast about the potential of flooding, as these higher-than-normal tides coincide with sea level rise caused by El Niño.
With files from Janella Hamilton and Philip Drost

articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who faced U.S. deportation efforts and 'vindictive prosecution,' arrives in Spain
articles.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the U.S., arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a…

image.caption: Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrives at Madrid's airport after leaving the United States, on Wednesday. (Francisco Seco/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the U.S., arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Trump administration celebrates 31-year-old's departure after nearly 2-year legal saga
Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to an El Salvador prison despite never having been convicted of a crime in the U.S.

Protracted legal battles ensued. A judge accused U.S. President Donald Trump's administration of "bad faith" when it said it was helpless to adhere a court order to return him from the notorious CECOT prison to the U.S.
Abrego Garcia was only returned in June 2025 when federal officials charged him with a series of offences including human smuggling in relation to a 2022 incident in Tennessee.

That case fell apart, with a federal judge this past May saying it reflected an "abuse of prosecuting power" from the government. He granted Abrego Garcia's motion to dismiss for "selective or vindictive prosecution."

Abrego Garcia and his wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura, right, leave the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in Greenbelt, Md., following a Oct. 6 hearing. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

Abrego Garcia, married and a father of a young child, later expressed his willingness to be deported to Costa Rica, which had agreed to accept him. However, the Trump administration refused, attempting to send him to Africa, part of its third-country deportation efforts that have been condemned by international human rights organizations.
Abrego Garcia, his lawyers and the Trump administration sought to portray the departure as a victory.

"I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom," Abrego Garcia said in a statement. "I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight."
Abrego Garcia didn't speak to reporters after landing at Madrid's main international airport on Wednesday, and raised a fist as he entered a van.

items: U.S. Supreme Court set to hear 3 major Trump agenda immigration cases

blocks.text: Lawyer hopes Abrego Garcia can return to U.S.

The Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that Abrego Garcia self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back in to the U.S.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was "delighted" about Abrego Garcia's departure, listing off a litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, called this a temporary departure as he "waits out the end of this administration." He said Abrego Garcia has many options to return to U.S.

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he said.
LISTEN | One of Abrego Garcia's lawyers spoke to CBC's As It Happens in 2025:
As It Happens6:24Trump's fixation on wrongly deported man's tattoos nothing but a distraction, says lawyer
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia at the El Salvadoran mega-prison, described him as a "free man" and said he is travelling to a country of his choice.
"I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration's constant persecution," he said in a statement.
The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has lived in Maryland for years as an unauthorized resident after entering the country as a teenager.

In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

Abrego Garcia's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport one million people annually. Democrats have slammed the efforts, pointing to widespread arrests of people not accused of committing a crime in the U.S. Deaths of individuals in immigration detention have also increased compared to past administrations.

When Abrego Garcia was deported, an official from the Trump administration called the move an "administrative error," but the president and El Salvador's autocratic leader Nayib Bukele celebrated the deportation of migrants from the U.S. to the Latin American prison. Trump encouraged Bukele to build more prisons.

The administration also widely communicated that Abrego Garcia's wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura, a U.S. citizen, sought a protection order from him in both 2020 and 2021. He was never arrested, and Vasquez Sura withdrew the order, saying the couple had entered counselling.

Later in Abrego Garcia's legal saga, Todd Lyons, then acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States."
Trump encourages El Salvador to build more prisons to house deportees from U.S.
Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.

His case took an unusual turn on Oct. 6 when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether ICE could detain and deport him to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.

blocks.text: When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was cancelled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation.

The U.S. Supreme Court is scheduled in the current session that runs through June 2027 to hear a number of cases that could alter the framework of the country's immigration and asylum system, including one that concerns third-country deportations.

blocks.text: Hockey·New
Russia’s legal win to return to international ice hockey will be challenged with an appeal at Switzerland’s supreme court, the sport’s governing body said Wednesday.
IIHF raises questions about the impartiality of 2 judges in case

The International Ice Hockey Federation raised questions about the impartiality of two of the three judges on a Court of Arbitration for Sport panel that ruled last month to end Russian teams’ exile imposed since the full military invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.
The Swiss Federal Tribunal can overturn CAS rulings - and send cases back for a retrial - on limited procedural grounds, such as the integrity of judges.
The Moroccan soccer body is expected to take a similar legal path after a CAS ruling Tuesday to reinstate Senegal as the Africa Cup of Nations champion.

“Given the significance of the ruling and its implications for international ⁠ice hockey,” the IIHF said Wednesday in a statement, it “considers it definitively essential to pursue the matter before the Swiss Federal Tribunal.”

Putin criticizes 'disregard' for sports ruling with Russia barred from Alberta world juniors

blocks.text: Swiss media reports suggested two judges hearing Russia’s appeal had traveled to Moscow for legal conferences in the past 18 months. Those reports appeared after the CAS verdict and too late to contest the appointment of judges, who are selected by the parties to the appeal and the court itself.

One of the CAS judges, Guilio Palermo, also cited on his legal firm’s website he was an investigator for the Russian-backed International Boxing Association led by Umar Kremlev, the oligarch now better known as a guest who helped bankroll the recent wedding of Donald Trump Jr.

The IIHF said its appeal to federal judges was “based on concerns around the independence and impartiality of two of the three arbitrators on the CAS Panel, especially following the information that has recently come to light regarding potential links between the two arbitrators and Russia.”
Russian hockey’s legal win at CAS has not guaranteed its teams can actually play in IIHF competitions.

items: IIHF confirms cyberattack after website goes offline
IIHF confirms Russia not competing at world juniors in Alberta

blocks.text: Canada has refused to let a Russian team enter the country for the men’s junior world championship next month. Several European ice hockey federations said they will boycott tournaments if Russia is allowed to play.
FIFA case set precedent for excluding Russian teams

The Russian hockey federation won its appeal at CAS despite the precedent of FIFA and UEFA winning a similar case at the sports court in 2022. FIFA lawyers cited inevitable chaos organizing a World Cup if Russia qualified and future opponents refused to play those games.

Challenging the integrity of a CAS judge before Swiss federal judges did work for Chinese swimming star Sun Yang who had been banned for eight years in 2019 at the sports court for violating doping rules.

Sun’s case was sent back to CAS for a retrial with a different panel of judges, which also found him guilty and banned him for four years. He also challenged that ban at the Swiss federal court and lost.
