articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.summary:
Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis…

blocks.text: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. Much of Gaza’s drinking water previously came from desalination plants and three Israeli-controlled pipelines, which were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

Ghoneim told a news conference that 272 meningitis infections had been reported in the territory in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. Fifteen Palestinians have died of meningitis since the beginning of this year, he said.

blocks.caption: A doctor examines a child suffering from meningitis at al-Rantisi children’s hospital in Gaza City. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilisation materials and fuel,” the health ministry said.

The UN’s humanitarian agency (Ocha) had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City.
Ocha said the increase in cases could be attributed to crowded tents and schools, the deterioration of shelter and sanitation conditions and exposure to unsafe water.
Gaza’s water crisis is severe. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s supply came from an aquifer that is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater, making it unfit for human consumption.

For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease. Acute diarrhoea is among the leading causes of illness in the territory. About 15,000 cubic metres a day of untreated waste seeps into the groundwater from soak-away pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.
The World Health Organization said in September that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

In addition to disease outbreaks and shortages of drinking water and basic necessities, Palestinians continue to face attacks and ceasefire violations by the Israeli military, which has intensified its strikes in recent days.

Soldiers crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza last Wednesday in the first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed in October last year, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Four people were killed and seven wounded in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the health ministry, bringing the death toll since the ceasefire took effect to 1,679.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 176,000 wounded since the beginning of the war in October 2023, according to Gaza’s health authorities.

articles.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
articles.summary: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's…

image.caption: Will the European Union soon have 28 members or more? Or will some member states block the accession of certain candidate countries?Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's been quite a while since the EU's last enlargement: Croatia was the last country to join the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another enlargement might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the European Union in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands.
EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time that something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of blackmail and a political weapon, paralyzing the EU in the process.

blocks.caption: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in October that Montenegro could become a member of the European Union in 2028Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.
Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands
Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.
As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

blocks.caption: Croatia is calling, among other things, for the return of the training ship Jadran, which used to belong to the Yugoslav Royal Navy and was based in Split (now Croatia) before the Yugoslav warsImage: Martin Vas/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.
Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.
Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. Ultimately, however, Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

blocks.caption: A poster for a petition organized by the previous Hungarian government against EU financial aid for Ukraine in March. The slogan reads 'Let's not let Zelenskyy have the last laugh'Image: Denes Erdos/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters, among other things after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.
North Macedonia: The never-ending blockade
No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.
The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.
But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.
Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

blocks.caption: A protest in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, against making any concessions to Bulgaria in 2022Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

blocks.text: Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.
Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.
Serbia: Croatia is not the only country obstructing progress
Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.
In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.
While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.
These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October after almost two years of anti-government, anti-corruption protests will change this situation is impossible to say.
Albania: Greece threatens to use minority rights as leverage
The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of the Greek minority, particularly relating to property rights, are adequately protected.
An end to the veto system?
In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.
The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

articles.title: CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed…

image.caption: Senegal won the trophy on the field, but Morocco were awarded the trophy after a CAF review of the events of the finalImage: Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."
The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."

"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.
"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."
An infamous AFCON final

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.
Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.
The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.
"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.
Why African football is changing the World Cup forever
Impact on future World Cup host
The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.

Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

articles.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
articles.summary:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.
“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”
Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.
“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”
The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”
No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.
Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”
The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.
It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

articles.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had only been in the position for two months, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's interior ministry says.

blocks.text: An Israeli air strike has killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said Naeem Abu Nahel was targeted by an aircraft in western Gaza City. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel had been "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
Earlier, Palestinian first responders and health officials reported that six other people had been killed in two Israeli air strikes elsewhere in Gaza on Tuesday.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, they said. The other three, including two police officers, were killed in a separate strike on a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, condemned the second attack, saying it was "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it had "struck terrorists in the area".
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed by Israel and Hamas in October last year.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Bombed factories, billion-dollar opportunity: Why German companies are staying in Ukraine
articles.summary: German companies remain committed to Ukraine despite million-dollar losses, an unreliable energy supply and a shortage of skilled workers. They are betting on new markets and long-term growth.

image.caption: Foreign companies operating in Ukraine see big opportunities, but also face substantial risksImage: Sergey Bobok/AFP

blocks.text: Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses and residential buildings: The massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under fire, affecting German companies.

"Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs said. "We are preparing for a difficult winter."
Made in Germany — Rebuilding Ukraine
Ukrainian economy under pressure
After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks."

Energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

"Not a single German company has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year."
EU releases €3.2 billion from Ukraine recovery fund
Benefits extend beyond Ukraine

Military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine and the software in Germany.

A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," he said.
Half a trillion dollars needed for reconstruction

For foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act. On the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following 10 years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Mechanical engineering, energy and infrastructure opportunities
"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin.

"German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted. However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks."
Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he added.
Investment guarantees and reforms as prerequisites for new projects

At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment."

Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.
High-tech revolution in defense
Who is financing Ukraine's reconstruction?

Representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: Companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the company and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different. When investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
articles.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than…

image.caption: One day green, the next day red — global stock markets have swung wildly in recent monthsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.
Will Anthropic put profits over security?
How passive investing is fueling the AI trade
The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

blocks.caption: The rise of neo-stock brokers, like Trade Republic in Europe, has spurred public interest in investingImage: Claudia Nass/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump has pressured TSMC to move some chip production from Taiwan to the USImage: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?
AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

articles.title: Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord
articles.summary: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops detained 'El Chapo Isidro', who had managed to evade capture for years.

blocks.text: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.
The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

articles.title: A teenage runaway turned to a Mountie for sanctuary. He had other plans
articles.summary: Kim Budd spent much of her childhood on the run. When she thought she'd finally found a safe place to stay it turned out to be anything but, and the adults and institutions that were supposed to…

image.caption: (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: On a bone-chilling night in January 1983, Kim Budd, just 15, sits in handcuffs at the Riverview RCMP detachment in a suburb of Moncton, N.B.
She's run away from home — again.
"I spent the whole night with them," recalled Budd, now 59 and living in western Quebec. "They locked me to a chair."

There's no mug shot and no charges because the teen has committed no crime. But the officer who picked her up off the frigid street isn't sure what to do with this runaway, and worries she'll bolt if she isn't restrained.
Tired and uncomfortable, the girl sits there until the morning shift arrives. One of the Mounties who has just come in pays her special attention.
"The first time I ever laid eyes on him I had a cold pit in the centre of my stomach," Budd recalled decades later. "He was sitting on the desk and he kept looking at me and watching me."
Budd, with her dark eyes and hair cut in an '80s shag, glares back with a scowl perfected by teenagers.
Then the Mountie approaches with an unexpected offer. He tells her he and his wife run an emergency foster home for kids like her. Would she like to stay with them?
The teen, who has already bounced from abusive home to group residence to reform school and then back to the same abusive home, agrees.
"He just wanted to help me. That's what I thought," she said.

In fact, the Mountie would demand much more from the troubled runaway, and the shelter and security he offered her would soon turn into a new form of confinement. She would learn that none of the adults who were supposed to protect her — not the police, not the doctors, not the child welfare officials — could be trusted when she needed them most, and the more she cried out for help, the less anyone would listen to the terrible truth she struggled to tell.
RCMP officer accused of abusing teen foster daughter
Kim Budd was a runner. She ran away from adults, and often into trouble.

Born in a small town along New Brunswick's Miramichi River, Budd was the youngest of six children and the only girl. Her father took off for good a few weeks later, leaving the family struggling financially.
Budd describes a difficult childhood, including being molested by a neighbour when she was four.
"I had some issues with that growing up," she said.
Her mother later remarried a man Budd remembers as volatile, strict and abusive.
"The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember," she said. "I was about nine or so, he would start putting his hands on my breasts or between my legs and he almost made it into a game."
Budd's step-father denies the abuse, and it's unclear what her mother, a woman Budd describes as passive and unaffectionate, actually knew over the years. She did not want to talk to CBC.
Budd first ran away from home at 13. 'The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember,' she told CBC. (Submitted)
By 13, Budd was starting to act out. She shoplifted, drank alcohol, experimented with drugs and hitchhiked, earning the label "juvenile delinquent."
Budd says in reality, she was shy, vulnerable and often frightened.
"I had some anger issues, but I wasn't tough," she said. "I didn't care whether I lived or died. I knew it was risky."
By the time she turned 14, her mother and step-father had had enough. They called New Brunswick's social services and the girl was placed in a group home, then reform school.
After 11 months at the Nova Scotia School for Girls in Truro, Budd was sent back to live with her mother and step-father. But that didn't last long.
"I needed to make some changes," Budd recalled. "My parents needed to make some changes…. They never recognized what they were doing that contributed to my running away."
So she ran again, and that's when the RCMP picked her up.

Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for about five years when he first encountered Kim Budd. Due to his standing in the community, he and his wife were quickly approved to be foster parents. (Submitted by Gilles Plouffe)
In 1983, Const. Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for four years and was already on his third posting.
Plouffe was fluently bilingual and stood over six feet tall with broad shoulders and a wispy mustache. As a kid he'd been an altar boy, a boy scout, an air cadet and a school crossing guard.
He married his high school sweetheart when they were still in their teens, and by 25 they were helping raise other people's children in addition to two young kids of their own.
In a system desperate for foster parents, the young couple was welcomed with open arms. He was an officer of the law, after all.
"I think they saw us as a blessing," he recalled in a recent interview with CBC. "They cut corners like you wouldn't believe. We didn't have any formal background check."
Soon, the Plouffe foster home became a handy option whenever the RCMP picked up a young person like Budd. They'd simply notify social services, and that was that.

Michel Cormier, a retired social worker in Moncton, N.B., stands near the Petitcodiac River in the early fall of 2026. Despite dealing with hundreds of cases over his career, he says he still remembers Kim Budd from the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Michel Cormier, a New Brunswick social worker tasked with overseeing the care of teens in the early 1980s, got that call the day Budd arrived at the Plouffe foster home.
Budd had been under Cormier's supervision during her months in group homes and reform school, and he can still remember her all these years later.
"She was a nice kid," Cormier told CBC. "I tried to respect her, not treat her like a juvenile delinquent — basically as a child that was in a difficult situation."
Placing Budd with the Plouffes seemed like an ideal solution.
"These were the perfect foster parents," Cormier recalled everyone thinking at the time. "This Disney kind of family, that everything was beautiful."
A recent photo of the house in Riverview, N.B., where Gilles Plouffe and his wife fostered children in the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Budd, a kid who had long dreamed of belonging to a "normal" family, settled in with the Plouffes and started Grade 9 at Riverview Junior High.
While her basement bedroom was being prepared, the teen slept on a pull-out couch.
One night when her foster mother was away, Gilles Plouffe came in wearing only a bathrobe and slipped under the covers with her.
"I kept falling asleep off and on, and he kept getting closer. And he had intercourse with me that night," Budd recalled. She remembers being afraid.
Plouffe apologized to the teen shortly after, telling her what happened had been an "accident." But the abuse continued, becoming more frequent and opportunistic.
"There was never a choice for me," Budd said. "He was my foster father and what he did to me that night, and the many times afterwards, was illegal."
While Plouffe disputes certain details, he now acknowledges he had sex on multiple occasions with the teenager in his care.
"It wasn't set out to be a predator looking for a prey," he told CBC. "I didn't mean to do anything bad, I just wanted to have a girlfriend."
Gilles Plouffe talked openly with CBC's Julie Ireton about his history with Kim Budd. He wore his RCMP-issue leather boots to the interview. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Now 69, Plouffe needed no convincing to talk openly with CBC about his history with Kim Budd. Plouffe's then wife, Budd's former foster mother, died in 2007.
During a lengthy interview, Plouffe showed no anger, hostility or concern. Rather, he appeared to welcome the opportunity to provide his own version of what happened in the foster home.

"It was a love connection," he insists. "And it's hard to say, 'Hey, you're a Mountie and you're supposed to enforce law and you're supposed to know better,' and all this kind of stuff. I know all that."
Plouffe acknowledged he was aware of the sexual abuse Budd had endured as a child and as a runaway.

"It's not like she hadn't done it before. OK, I said it. It's not nice to say that, but she did do it before," said Plouffe. "I was showing her that people could be gentle, that it wasn't like the truckers she had met while running, that she could be passed on as a slave from one truck to the next."
The way he tells it, he provided the teen with food, shelter, clothing and "good values."
And yet he was keenly aware that what he was doing to his foster daughter was illegal.

Every male person who has illicit sexual intercourse with his step-daughter, foster daughter or female ward ... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.Section 153, Criminal Code of Canada c. 1983

Back then, Section 153 of the Criminal Code clearly stated that a man who has "illicit sexual intercourse with his foster daughter … is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years." (Today the crime falls under sexual exploitation.)
"I had the Criminal Code in the house, and I showed her," said Plouffe. "I told her, as a Mountie, I had no intention of going into jail. That's the last place any police officer wants to end up."
"He showed me in the book that he could go to prison," Budd recalled. "He just thought he was above the law."
The abuse continued. But almost two years into her stay with the Plouffes, it's Budd who would find herself in handcuffs once again, being taken away in a police car.
Two days after Christmas 1984, Budd, by then 17, got into a heated argument with her foster mother.
"She started going on and on about responsibility," Budd recalled. "She had been irresponsible in my view. She wasn't being a responsible wife and I had to have sex with her husband."
The argument escalated and the woman threw a slice of pizza in Budd's face, then ran to her bedroom.
Budd followed. She had had enough of the lying and sneaking around, and of her foster father's late night visits. She was going to reveal the secret.
"I was running to tell her that Gilles had been sleeping with me," Budd said.
But Gilles Plouffe was right behind her.
"He grabbed me and put the chokehold on me and he made me unconscious," Budd said.
When she came to she was handcuffed, put in the back of Plouffe's RCMP cruiser and driven to the Moncton Hospital.
Moncton Hospital documents from December 1984 and early 1985 detailed Budd's admission, diagnosis and discharge. CBC has redacted some private information. (Submitted)
Hospital documents from December 1984 confirm that Budd arrived in restraints and that Plouffe told hospital staff the teen had "threatened to kill his family."
"Foster father is an RCMP officer. He used force to subdue her," the emergency admission form notes. "He feels the death threats are real."
Budd insists the only threat she'd made was to tell her foster mother that her husband had been having sex with her.

The 17-year-old was admitted to the adult psychiatric ward where she was medicated, underwent tests and attended group therapy. The hospital psychologist noted that Budd was insecure, impulsive, angry and suicidal, and that she felt "unloved" and had a "strong need for affection."

A couple weeks into her hospital stay, Budd disclosed to the staff psychologist what was really happening in the foster home. Documents from the time refer to Budd's "alleged accusations" but provide no details.
"I just needed to get it out. I needed the sex to stop," Budd recalled telling the psychologist.
Then she told Plouffe what she had done. That forced him to admit the truth to his wife.

Budd spent three weeks in the psychiatric ward of the Moncton Hospital when she was still 17. She told a hospital psychologist here that her foster father had been abusing her. (Marc Grandmaison/The Canadian Press)
The psychologist summoned the Plouffes to the hospital for a meeting. Eventually, Budd was brought into the room.
"They told me never to talk to anyone about the abuse that had happened in their home," she said. "They made me promise."
Looking back, Budd says staff at the hospital never regarded her as a child, but as a mistress.
"I had a nurse reprimand me: ‘How dare you sleep with a married man?' So she blamed me for the abuse, and that's pretty much how I got blamed for what happened, instead of Gilles."
The teenager had endured two years of abuse in her foster home. She'd finally worked up the courage to tell someone in a position of authority. And then the adults colluded against her.
Plouffe said he informed child welfare authorities that he and his wife would no longer be fostering children, but no one reported the abuse to the RCMP.
"I didn't ask anybody to cover anything," Plouffe insists. "I don't know. They see me as a Mountie. What are you going to do?"
Budd models a borrowed outfit for an upcoming job interview. (Submitted)

In fact, in yet another incredible twist, Budd — not Plouffe — would find herself in trouble with the law once again, this time as part of a spurious murder claim made by her abuser in January 1984, shortly after she was hospitalized.
"She had told [us] that she had killed somebody," Plouffe told CBC.

While the details remain vague, Plouffe said Budd had admitted to him that she'd killed a trucker in the U.S. after he had "taken advantage of her." He told his superiors at the RCMP and an investigator was assigned to the case.
Today, Budd calls it all a fiction concocted by Plouffe to distract his superiors from what was really happening to her in the foster home.
"I've never killed anybody — never," Budd said. "Gilles made me go through and told me to tell them."
But at the time, Budd, still just 17, went along with the ruse.
"I was just trying to protect Gilles," she said. "It's hard to explain it now, but I was a shell."
RCMP files confirm an investigation in 1984, but no charges were laid and the case was quickly closed when no evidence was found to corroborate Budd's confession.
Still, the teen was now firmly under Plouffe's control, as though handcuffed once again.
Budd and Plouffe married in 1988 and moved from New Brunswick back to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que. (Submitted)
Budd was released from hospital in the winter of 1984 and went back to live with her mother and step-father. She dropped out of school and worked nights cleaning offices.
Before long, Plouffe, now separated from his wife, reappeared. He would turn up suddenly in his police vehicle, letting Budd know he was never far away.
"He was supposed to stay away from me, but he never did," she said. "I couldn't go to the RCMP because he was the RCMP."
Budd knew she couldn't run again.
"I believed he could have found me anywhere," she recalled. "I was afraid he was going to make me disappear…. He had weapons at the house, in his police car."
Eventually, she relented to his frequent calls. The sex continued.
"I can't explain the hold Gilles had over me," Budd said. "He didn't court me. We didn't go to movies or restaurants, he didn't buy me gifts. I was his toy."
Shortly after turning 18, Budd moved in with Plouffe and his two young children. When her former foster mother found out she became furious, and this time went to the police.
Gilles Plouffe tells his side of the story

The RCMP began an investigation in 1986, according to documents obtained by CBC. Plouffe's police colleagues set out to determine if the sexual relationship had started while Budd was still in foster care.
They never talked to the alleged perpetrator, however.
"They did not interview me. They interviewed Kim," Plouffe confirmed. "But they never asked me if I did anything wrong."

It's unclear whether the RCMP questioned anyone at New Brunswick's child protection services, which oversees foster care in the province. And yet both Plouffe and former social worker Michel Cormier confirmed that employees within the department knew about what had gone on in the Plouffe home.

"The people that knew, I imagine probably had the idea that it was not any of their business. So they didn't go forward with a complaint to the police like it should have been done," Cormier said. (He left the agency shortly after Budd's placement with the Plouffes, but later returned to work there part-time.)

New Brunswick's Social Development office is responsible for child protective services including foster care. Budd was a ward of the province when she was in foster care in the early 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
According to Budd, Plouffe coached her to tell anyone who asked that the sex had started after she turned 18.
"He kept telling me that if I told his lie often enough, it would become my truth," she said.
Once again, the teen lied for Plouffe and the RCMP wrapped up the investigation.

"The allegation that Cst. Plouffe had sexual intercourse with Kimberly Ann Budd while she was a ward of Cst. Plouffe is unsubstantiated. There is no evidence to support this fact and no way we will ever be able to prove this fact," states an RCMP memo from August 1986.
But Plouffe's association with this teen runaway and one-time murder suspect created a new problem for him: He was deemed a security risk – not because of anything he'd done, but because of her.

"His security clearance has been downgraded," states the memo. "We do not feel there is any further action to be taken at this point with the exception of verifying periodically if Budd becomes involved in her former activities."
Budd became pregnant with her first child at 19. She and Plouffe would have three sons together. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Budd was 19 when she became pregnant with her first child, giving birth to a baby boy in May 1987. She would go on to have two more sons with her former foster father.
"I was very trapped," she said.
With no proposal or engagement ring, Budd and Plouffe married in a civil ceremony in January 1988 at the Moncton courthouse. No friends or family attended, and Plouffe did not wear his red serge.
"They harassed him about it until he quit the RCMP," Budd said, suggesting that despite dropping their investigation, Plouffe's superiors may have had their suspicions.
Later that same year the newlyweds left New Brunswick and moved to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que., initially moving in with his mother.
There, years later during a therapy session for one of their children, Budd told the therapist about the origins of her relationship with Plouffe.
"She kept giving me cards to go see a women's shelter," said Budd. "I started looking at my marriage … how dysfunctional it was."

At 27 — 12 years after first meeting him — Budd finally left Plouffe for good. She took computer courses and eventually secured a job with the federal government where she remained for more than 20 years.

RCMP officer Sandra Lavallee interviews Budd at the national police force's Ottawa office in 2017. During the interview, Budd reported the sexual abuse she suffered as a teen in the Plouffe foster home. CBC obtained a video of the interview through an access to information request. (RCMP)
In April 2017, Budd sat in an RCMP interview room in Ottawa to detail her complaint against Gilles Plouffe for historical sexual abuse.
In a video of that interview, Budd's pain is raw. Through tears, she recounts what she went through between the ages of 15 and 17 in the Plouffe foster home.
"He told me that I couldn't tell anyone. Nobody would understand ... it was our secret," Budd told the interviewer.
Shortly after, RCMP Const. Simon Boucher of New Brunswick's Codiac detachment launched an investigation.
Kim Budd speaks with reporter Julie Ireton outside the RCMP offices in Ottawa where in 2017 Budd reported the abuse she suffered in the 1980s. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

CBC obtained through access to information the interview video and close to 400 pages of documents related to the 2017 investigation. While much has been redacted, the police files note that Boucher searched "different databases" for witnesses including Budd's former social worker, Michel "Mike" Cormier.

"The attempt to contact Mike Cormier … were negative," the records state. "Cst. Boucher followed up with social services in Moncton, no one from their office are aware of a Mike Cormier that worked there between 1980 and 1990."
Yet CBC easily found Cormier through social media. He still lives in the Moncton area, and during several conversations shared what he knows about Budd's childhood.
Cormier said he would have given the RCMP the same information — including the open secret about what went on at the Plouffe home — had an investigator ever called to ask.
Despite the RCMP's claim that it couldn't find him in 2017, Michel Cormier was still living in New Brunswick and employed as a social worker at a Moncton hospital. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
The RCMP closed the investigation into Budd's complaint in August 2018.
"There is not enough likelihood of conviction," Boucher concluded. "The main issue in the matter is the reliability and credibility of KB because there is no eye witness to the alleged sexual acts."
But there was another eye witness: Gilles Plouffe. Yet the RCMP never contacted him, reducing what Boucher called a case of "he said, she said" to a simple matter of "she said."

Plouffe spent hours talking openly with CBC about his past, demonstrating that he's not shy to discuss what happened in his foster home in the early 1980s. But he said he was never aware of the RCMP investigation until told about it by CBC.
Once again, Budd had tried to tell the truth, only to be dismissed.
"There was evidence there that he had abused me. They just ignored it," said Budd.

Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa, reviewed Kim Budd's legal files. 'We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying,' she told CBC. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

"There's no other victim where we assume that they are lying about what happened to them. That is unique to sexual assault, still today," said Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa who reviewed the legal documents in Budd's case.
"We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying."
Gilbert thinks Michel Cormier's evidence could have made a difference.

"I am embarrassed for the RCMP that they couldn't find him," she said. "Even without him testifying, the RCMP speaking to him and hearing that she had disclosed her sexual abuse, I would have thought would have been a persuasive reason to lay a charge."
RCMP Const. Simon Boucher was "not able to do an interview" with CBC, according to the force's media relations officer in New Brunswick.

According to Sunny Marriner, national lead for the Improving Institutional Accountability Project, investigators displayed "textbook behaviour" when they claimed Budd was an unreliable witness because as a teen she'd lied, done drugs and run away.

"Children who are experiencing sexual abuse may withdraw. They begin to have difficulty attending school or engaging in activities. They frequently run away," she said. "It doesn't undermine credibility, it supports that something was happening to the child at that time."
'It wasn't abuse, it was love,' Plouffe said of his relationship with Budd when she was still in her teens and he was her foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Decades later, Gilles Plouffe still frames what happened in his foster home not as abuse, but as a love story.
"It's wrong, but that doesn't mean we have to go and and really shove it down my throat and say that was really wrong, beat me on the head," Plouffe said. "It wasn't abuse, it was love.”
That's a story Marriner says she's heard before in her work with survivors.

"It is not love, it is exploitation," she said. "Many people will be familiar with the term grooming.… It means very slowly creating a bond with the person that you intend to exploit that makes them believe that the two of you are on the same team together against the entire world."
Looking back, Budd realizes the odds were stacked against her.
"He got away with it because he was in the RCMP, so it got covered up for him and he got protected and he'll never be charged," she said.
Budd, right, shows Ireton the statement of claim in her case against her former foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
In the spring of 2019, Budd filed a lawsuit against the province of New Brunswick, the Moncton Hospital, the regional health authority and Gilles Plouffe.
"Plouffe was given the power and duty to discipline and punish the plaintiff, which he used to perpetrate the physical, emotional and sexual abuse," noted the statement of claim.
The lawsuit alleged the institutions were negligent and the hospital psychologist breached his fiduciary duty by failing to report the sexual abuse to the RCMP.

Those institutions denied all allegations, and in formal statements of defence noted that any injury, loss or damages suffered by the plaintiff were no fault of theirs. They also declined to talk to CBC about the case.
In July 2026 a judge at the Moncton Court of King's Bench heard a trial for damages against Gilles Plouffe. A decision is pending. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
There was no trial, and in 2024 the suit was resolved out of court. Details are not public.

Plouffe didn't defend himself against the claim and in November 2019 was found in default — the civil court's way of saying he didn't bring forward any evidence to deny the allegation that he repeatedly sexually abused, assaulted and molested Budd for two years, starting when she was 15.
This July, the Court of King's Bench in Moncton heard a trial for damages in the case of Kimberly Anne Budd vs. Joseph Yves Gilles Plouffe.

"I want his acknowledgement. I want some accountability for it," said Budd, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder and a persistent depressive disorder — conditions that will require treatment for the rest of her life.
Budd and her lawyer are still waiting for the judge's decision in the case.
Kim Budd says she hopes her family will now understand her past
Plouffe has never acknowledged that what he did changed the course of a teen girl's life, and no one has ever asked him to. Marrying Budd and having children with her didn't change anything.
For two years, between the ages of 15 and 17, she was a child and her foster parents were in charge. Institutions failed her, and worse, sought to discredit her when she tried to tell them the truth.

Gilles Plouffe's position with the police gave him privilege and standing in the community. The reaction of the systems intended to protect children exemplifies the entitlement he enjoyed as an officer.
It's why Budd feels she has to keep telling her side of the story, over and over again.
"Some people might call it revenge, but it's not — it's justice," said Budd. "I want the record set straight."
Budd's story is tragic, and repeating it is embarrassing and painful, but she realized long ago that she needed to stop running from it.
"I want my kids to hear it. They're old enough now they can process it … and they can make their decisions."
Kim Budd was a troubled teenager, a vulnerable kid whose imperfections placed her in a perfect position to be victimized over and over again.
Today, she's a survivor.
If you need help: Sexual Assault Centres, Crisis Lines, and Support Service in Canada

articles.title: Russian drone violates Polish airspace days after cruise missiles fell on country – Europe live
articles.summary:
Authorities investigating ‘intentional activity’ amid growing tensions between Moscow and countries on Nato’s eastern flank

Meanwhile, the Financial Times is reporting this morning…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 17m agoUS delaying delivery of much-needed Patriot air defence missiles - media report
27m agoMorning opening: Poland investigating (another) brief airspace violation by Russian drone

blocks.text: US delaying delivery of much-needed Patriot air defence missiles - media report
Meanwhile, the Financial Times is reporting this morning that the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of about 60 much-needed Patriot air defence interceptors to Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian service members walk next to a launcher of a Patriot air defence system, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in an undisclosed location, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: The interceptors, paid for by Ukraine’s western allies, are reportedly being held up by the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, who needs to sign off on their re-export, three people told the newspaper.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has repeatedly warned of the urgent need for more air defence missiles to protect the skies above Ukraine as the country braces for a difficult winter, with Russia continuing its strikes on critical civilian infrastructure.
Morning opening: Poland investigating (another) brief airspace violation by Russian drone

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

A suspected Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during strikes on western Ukraine on Monday night in what authorities have described as “intentional activity” by Moscow – just days after three cruise missiles fell in Poland during a major attack on Ukraine.
The drone, believed to be carrying surveillance equipment, remained in Polish airspace for eight minutes before flying back to Ukraine.
Poland’s deputy defence minister, Paweł Zalewski, told RMF24 that the military decided against shooting it down because of risks to civilian properties in the area.

The incident took place just hours after Nato held emergency talks over last week’s airspace breach, authorising the deployment of a Nato Airborne Warning and Control System, AWACS, aircraft to Poland.

It also comes amid growing tensions between Russia and countries on the eastern flank of Nato, with Moscow making unsubstantiated accusations against Estonia warning that it’s acting ‘on verge of unleashing open war,” and a growing diplomatic spat with Finland.
Overnight, at least two people were killed and 40 injured in Russian attacks on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia ⁠overnight, with further attacks reported in the Sumy region.
I will keep an eye on this for you.
It’s Tuesday, 24 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
articles.summary:
Saurav Das was due to give talks at UK universities on protest movement but says ‘coward government’ prevented him flying

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.

Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.
The incident comes a month after he was detained for defying a security crackdown in Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.

“This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE (London School of Economics), Edinburgh to deliver talks on the Cockroach movement,” Das said in a social media post late on Monday. “Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual government was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions.”
Das was due to speak at the Oxford Union society on 1 December.
CJP-organised protests in July over alleged examination irregularities forced the education minister to resign, marking a rare climbdown by the government of Narendra Modi.

Critics say human rights and press freedoms have declined since Modi came to power in 2014. Earlier this month, India barred more than 100 foreign speakers from attending a democracy summit organised by the opposition Congress party. Those denied visas included a Norwegian journalist who had previously questioned Modi about press freedom.
